newsitem.title: USA: Brush, wind fuel Los Angeles national forest blaze.
newsitem.headline: Brush, wind fuel Los Angeles national forest blaze.

text.p: More than 2,000 firefighters continued on Monday to battle a 12,500-acre (4,900-hectare) blaze in the Angeles National Forest that was being fueled by tinder-dry brush and fanned by shifting winds.

The fire was 55 percent contained, but there was no estimate of when crews would have it under full control. Authorities say it was started last week by a backpacker who burned toilet paper to dispose of it instead of burying it, as the U.S. Forestry Service recommends.

Forestry Service spokeswoman Susie Wood said 2,200 firefighters were battling the flames, backed by 137 fire engines, seven bulldozers, 18 water-dropping helicopters, five air tankers and 24 water trucks.

Wood said the danger of the fire's spreading to the town of Wrightwood, a community of 4,000 people about 40 miles (65 km) northeast of Los Angeles, had abated. But fire engines were still being stationed in the town in case the winds pushed the flames in that direction, she added.
The fire came within two miles (3.2 km) of the town over the weekend but was stopped in its tracks by crews who started controlled backfires to deprive it of further fuel.
"As we gain more control over the fire, we expect to start moving those units (fire engines) out of the town," Wood said.

Five firefighters have sustained minor injuries, but so far no buildings or homes have been lost, Wood said. The fire was concentrated in steep mountain canyons in an area known as the Sheep Mountain Wilderness, she said.
